messages.author: 89a4640ddc6e46d0
messages.subject: Using MCMC Posterior as a Prior Distribution?
parts:
Hi,

I haven't been able to find an answer for this. But I think I am no asking this question correctly... hopefully someone can help.

I am trying to perform a power calculation. I have run my model with existing data, and have generated a posterior. I would now like to run the same model with "fake" data, using my posterior as a prior.

I realize I can do this with the generated quantities block. But ideally I want to be able to save my posterior, and then be able to use it as a prior in the future without re-running my original model. I'd also like to be able to share the posterior with others.

Is this possible?

Thanks

Mark

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using MCMC Posterior as a Prior Distribution?
parts:
It helps to write everything out mathematically.
I believe you have a model

p(y,theta) = p(theta|y) p(theta),

along with real data y and fake data y' and what
you'd like to do is calculate a sequential posterior

p(theta|y') propto p(y'|theta) p(theta|y)

where p(theta|y) is the posterior for the model with data y.

Because

p(theta|y) propto p(y|theta) p(theta)

this reduces to

p(theta|y, y') propto p(y|theta) p(y'|theta) p(theta)

You can just write the joint model for that.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using MCMC Posterior as a Prior Distribution?
parts:
You probably want to use a beta-binomial rather than
explicitly modeling theta[i]. And why cut a and b off at 1?

If you want to generate fake data based on the ongoing fit,
all you need to do is have:

data {
int N_sim;
int total[N_sim];
...

generated quantities {
int success_sim[N_sim];
for (int n in 1:N_sim)
success_sim[n] <- beta_binomial_rng(total[n], a, b);
}

You could alternately take the totals and N_sim to be
the same as in the observed data.

If there's some other quantity you want, could you try to
write it out mathematically?

- Bob

parts:
Hi,

I was trying to simplify my question, but I think I have confused the matter.

I am doing a bivariate meta-analysis of a diagnostic test (doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2005.02.022)

I have 2 studies. for each I have the true positives, false negatives, true negatives, true positives. My model is below

I want to determine the properties of a new studies needed to change my posterior distribution of LR_neg.

The sequential posterior concept, would it work if I just run this model twice:
1) first with just the 2 studies
2) second with the 2 studies, and my "fake" study to see if it change my conclusions?

or do I have to do something different to use the sequential posterior concept?



data{
int <lower=1> Nstudy;
int <lower=1> TP [Nstudy];
int <lower=1> TN [Nstudy];
vector [Nstudy] var_logit_spec;
vector [Nstudy] var_logit_sens;
int diseased [Nstudy];
int healthy [Nstudy];
real <lower=0> gam_a;
real <lower=0> gam_b;
}
parameters{
vector <lower=-10,upper=10> [2] mu_prior;
vector [2]  mu [Nstudy];
vector <lower=0> [2] tau;
real <lower=-1,upper=0> rho;
}
transformed parameters{
matrix[2,2] cov_prior [Nstudy];
vector [Nstudy] sens;
vector [Nstudy] spec;
real covar;
real sens_overall;
real spec_overall;

sens_overall<-inv_logit(mu_prior[1]);
spec_overall<-inv_logit(mu_prior[2]);

for (study in 1:Nstudy){
sens[study]<-inv_logit(mu[study,1]);
spec[study]<-inv_logit(mu[study,2]);
}

for (study in 1:Nstudy){
cov_prior[study,1,1]<-tau[1]+var_logit_sens[study];
cov_prior[study,1,2]<-rho*sqrt(tau[1]*tau[2]);
cov_prior[study,2,1]<-cov_prior[study,1,2];
cov_prior[study,2,2]<-tau[2]+var_logit_spec[study];
}

covar<-rho*tau[1]*tau[2];
}
model{
tau~inv_gamma(gam_a,gam_b);

for (study in 1:Nstudy){
mu [study] ~ multi_normal(mu_prior, cov_prior[study]);
TP[study]~binomial(diseased[study], sens[study]);
TN[study]~binomial(healthy[study], spec[study]);
}
}
generated quantities{
real LR_neg;
LR_neg<-(1-sens_overall)/spec_overall;
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using MCMC Posterior as a Prior Distribution?
parts:
This'd all be much easier to read if it was indented.

I'm still not sure what you mean by properties of a new
study needed to change your posterior. Any new study will
change the posterior. If it has exactly the same data
as the first study, the posterior intervals will become
narrower.

If you want to compare posteriors, just run one time with
the first set of data then a second time with the two sets of
data combined.

The point of sequential Bayesian inference is that it lets you
break apart observations into batches so you get the same answer
by updating a batch at a time, each time using the previous posterior
as a prior, as you would've gotten by just combining all the data
up front.

- Bob

Krushcke's blog, check out his recommendations at:

http://doingbayesiandataanalysis.blogspot.com/2015/01/how-to-specify-informed-prior-in.html

Quick summary: use a posterior sample to compute a
mean and covariance and then use the sample estimates as
parameters in a multi-normal prior.

- Bob
